lessons.title: Marketing and the marketing mix
lessons.html:
What marketing is

Marketing is not only selling. It is everything a farmer does to find out what buyers want, produce it, get it to them and be paid a good price. Good marketing starts before planting: a farmer who plants without knowing who will buy may end up with a crop nobody wants, or a price that does not cover costs.

Know your customer

  • Who buys your product? Households, spaza shops, hawkers, schools, restaurants, supermarkets, processors, fresh produce markets, exporters.
  • What do they want? Size, quality, packaging, quantity, delivery times, certification.
  • How much will they pay, and how and when do they pay?

The marketing mix: the four Ps

PQuestionsExample: free-range eggs
ProductWhat exactly are we selling? Quality, grade, packaging, brandClean, graded eggs in labelled trays of 30 and boxes of 6
PriceWhat will buyers pay? Do we cover our costs?Price checked against shops nearby and against cost per tray
PlaceWhere and how does the product reach buyers?Farm gate, two local shops, weekly delivery to a guesthouse
PromotionHow do buyers find out about us?Signboard on the road, WhatsApp group, samples at the shops

Market research made simple

  • Visit shops and markets. Note products, prices and quality.
  • Talk to buyers. Ask what they struggle to get.
  • Check fresh produce market prices and trends.
  • Talk to extension officers and other farmers.

Write down what you learn. Use it to decide what to grow, how much, and when to have it ready.

lessons.title: Marketing channels, pricing and keeping buyers
lessons.html:
Marketing channels

A marketing channel is the route a product takes from the farm to the final consumer.

ChannelAdvantagesDisadvantages
Farm gate or roadside stallCash, no transport, keeps full priceSmall volumes, time spent selling
Hawkers and informal tradersBuy small and medium amounts, often cashPrices vary, little security
Fresh produce market (through an agent)Takes large volumes, price set daily by supply and demandTransport costs, commission, price can drop
SupermarketsLarge, regular ordersStrict quality, certification and delivery rules; payment after delivery
Processors and contractsAgreed price or formula, planned volumesMust meet contract terms
Livestock auctionsOpen competition between buyersTransport, commission, animal stress

Many farmers use more than one channel to spread risk.

Setting a price

  1. Know your cost per unit (per kg, per tray, per animal). Add up all costs and divide by the quantity.
  2. Know the market price buyers pay elsewhere.
  3. Your price must cover costs and leave a profit, but stay attractive compared with competitors.
  4. Higher quality, reliable supply and good service can earn a better price.

Example: it costs R42 to produce a tray of 30 eggs. Shops nearby sell for R70 and buy from suppliers at about R58. Selling to shops at R55 to R58 covers costs and leaves a profit of R13 to R16 per tray.

Getting the product ready

  • Harvest at the right stage.
  • Grade by size and quality; remove damaged produce.
  • Pack in clean, suitable containers and label them.
  • Keep produce cool and deliver on time.

Keeping buyers

Supply what you promised, when you promised, at the agreed quality. Communicate early if there is a problem. A reliable supplier is valued and often gets repeat orders and better terms.

Key points

  • Marketing starts before production: find out what buyers want.
  • Use the four Ps: product, price, place and promotion.
  • Choose marketing channels and spread risk across more than one.
  • Price must cover cost per unit and stay competitive.
  • Grade, pack and deliver reliably to keep buyers.
